title: Judges 14:1–9
context: Judges 14 follows Samson as he sees and insists on marrying a Philistine woman of Timnah, against his parents’ covenantal objection. The narrator adds that this was of the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines then ruling Israel. On the way, the Spirit empowers Samson to kill a lion, and he later takes honey from its carcass, concealing the source from his parents. The passage holds together Samson’s flawed choices, the tension with his Nazirite calling, and God’s purpose working through them.

verses.text: Samson went down to Timnah, and saw a woman in Timnah of the daughters of the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samson goes down to Timnah and sees a Philistine woman. The story turns on what Samson sees and wants.

Arminian readers see Samson’s desire as his own choice, shaping the events that follow. Sight leading to desire is a recurring theme in his story.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrative notes Samson’s looking without yet commenting on it. Timnah lies in contested borderland.

Reformed readers see a gifted deliverer whose desires are not yet governed by his calling. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, preparing for the parents’ objection.

verses.text: He came up, and told his father and his mother, saying, “I have seen a woman in Timnah of the daughters of the Philistines. Now therefore get her for me as my wife.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Samson tells his parents he has seen a Philistine woman and demands that they get her as his wife. His request is abrupt.

Arminian readers see a son asserting his will over family and covenant concerns.
verses.reformedNotes:
The story assumes the parents will arrange the marriage. Samson asks them to act, but on his terms.

Reformed readers see impulsive desire directing his decisions. Both traditions read this with moral clarity, without excusing Samson and without cynicism toward the larger story God is telling.

verses.text: Then his father and his mother said to him, “Isn’t there a woman among your brothers’ daughters, or among all my people, that you go to take a wife of the uncircumcised Philistines?” Samson said to his father, “Get her for me, for she pleases me well.”
verses.arminianNotes:
His parents ask why he will not marry an Israelite rather than one of the uncircumcised Philistines; Samson says, “Get her for me, for she pleases me well.” Their objection is covenantal.

Arminian readers see Samson choosing personal preference over his parents’ godly counsel.
verses.reformedNotes:
The parents voice a concern rooted in Israel’s covenant identity, akin to Deuteronomy 7:3–4. Samson’s reply is literally that she is right in his eyes.

Reformed readers hear an echo of Judges’ refrain that everyone did what was right in his own eyes (17:6; 21:25). Both traditions share this reading.

verses.text: But his father and his mother didn’t know that it was of the LORD; for he sought an occasion against the Philistines. Now at that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The parents did not know that this was of the LORD, who sought an occasion against the Philistines ruling Israel. God is at work in the situation.

Arminian readers commonly say God foresaw and permitted Samson’s self-chosen path and then used it for his purpose, without approving or causing the sinful desire. Both traditions affirm that God is sovereign over history, that he is not the author of sin, and that Samson remains responsible.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator reveals what the parents could not see. God’s purpose stands behind events they opposed.

Reformed readers commonly say God ordained the course of events, including Samson’s choices, as the means to that purpose, without coercing his will or excusing it. Both traditions agree that God brings good purposes out of flawed human actions, and each tradition contains a range of formulations.

verses.text: Then Samson went down to Timnah with his father and his mother, and came to the vineyards of Timnah; and behold, a young lion roared at him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samson goes down to Timnah with his parents and, at the vineyards, a young lion roars at him. The setting in vineyards may be significant for a Nazirite.

Arminian readers note the tension between Samson’s calling and the places his choices take him.
verses.reformedNotes:
The vineyards recall the Nazirite ban on vine products. The text does not say Samson ate or drank there.

Reformed readers likewise avoid overreading but notice the detail. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with the lion’s attack setting up the first display of the Spirit’s power.

verses.text: The LORD’s Spirit came mightily on him, and he tore him as he would have torn a young goat with his bare hands, but he didn’t tell his father or his mother what he had done.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Spirit comes mightily on Samson, and he tears the lion apart with his bare hands, but tells neither parent. His strength comes from God.

Arminian readers see the Spirit empowering Samson despite his questionable path. Gifting is not the same as approval.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Spirit’s power is decisive; Samson’s strength is not his own. His secrecy introduces a pattern of concealment.

Reformed readers see God working through flawed instruments. Both traditions agree that the Spirit’s empowerment here does not endorse Samson’s choices.

verses.text: He went down and talked with the woman, and she pleased Samson well.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samson goes down and talks with the woman, and she pleases him well. His desire is confirmed.

Arminian readers see Samson proceeding without regard to his parents’ counsel or his calling.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase about her pleasing him echoes verse 3. The narrator keeps the focus on Samson’s own judgment.

Reformed readers see the narrative highlighting what governs Samson’s choices. Both traditions read this with moral clarity and without sensationalism, noting that the story will expose the cost of these choices.

verses.text: After a while he returned to take her, and he went over to see the carcass of the lion; and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey.
verses.arminianNotes:
Later, returning to marry her, Samson turns aside to see the lion’s carcass and finds bees and honey in it. Curiosity draws him to the dead body.

Arminian readers note that the Nazirite rules forbade contact with a dead person (Numbers 6:6), and touching an unclean animal’s carcass was itself defiling (Leviticus 11:27).
verses.reformedNotes:
Some readers see this as compromising Samson’s consecration, though Numbers 6 speaks specifically of human corpses.

Reformed readers likewise note the tension. Both traditions read it carefully and with moral clarity, without claiming more than the text states.

verses.text: He took it into his hands, and went on, eating as he went. He came to his father and mother and gave to them, and they ate, but he didn’t tell them that he had taken the honey out of the lion’s body.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samson scoops out the honey, eats as he goes, and gives some to his parents without telling them its source. His secrecy continues.

Arminian readers see concealment as a sign that Samson knew the act was questionable.
verses.reformedNotes:
He shares the honey but hides its origin from his parents. The concealment involves them unknowingly in uncleanness.

Reformed readers see how compromise can draw others in. Both traditions read this with moral clarity, and both note that the episode becomes the basis for the riddle that follows.
